paragraphs: I read people before I design for them. The instinct that matters most in UX — interrogate the system before proposing a solution — is the hardest skill in the job, and it does not come from a bootcamp or a tool. It comes from watching what users actually do when incentives, constraints and reality collide.

UX didn’t hijack my career. Research arrived before the title did. The questions are always the same — who are these people, what are they trying to do, who benefits from the current arrangement, and why does it keep failing the exact same way?

So when a checkout keeps dropping users and every stakeholder blames price, I go look at the screen. When an app keeps confusing new users, I go watch them use it. When someone asks me to “make it delightful,” I default to making it *defensible* instead.
polisci: Interrogating the brief, not obeying it
ux: Challenging the brief, not obeying it
about.pivot: I’ve always been drawn to studying systems. XR lets me build them. When the interface stops being a rectangle and becomes a place you walk into, the research-to-build loop gets brutally honest — you step inside the thing you’re designing. I trained in VR/AR at IIT Delhi because flat screens taught me layout, and I want to be inside the next decade of interfaces, not watching it from outside.

items.body: SaaS, e-commerce and real-estate products. Journey mapping, A/B testing, heuristic evaluation, Figma design systems, Agile/Scrum and dev handoff that developers actually thank me for.
End-to-end e-commerce and retail UI systems for repeat clients. Full discovery — personas, journey maps, wireframes — delivered mobile-first and WCAG 2.1 AA.
VR/AR, immersive workflow design, Unity prototyping, Blender modelling and environments, interactive VR experiences and simulations.
The research instinct most designers fake. Reading systems, people and incentives before proposing a single solution.
Where the habit of interrogating received wisdom started.
